trajectory.content: Lisa Su AMD CEO compensation fiscal 2026

AMD’s 2026 proxy statement reports that Chair, President and CEO Lisa Su received **$55,161,779 in total compensation for fiscal 2025**; this is the most recently disclosed CEO-pay figure in AMD’s FY2026 proxy, rather than compensation for fiscal 2026 itself. [[1, 2]] 

The reported total comprised **$1,291,258 salary**, **$41,669,390 stock awards**, **$8,951,513 option awards**, **$3,125,430 non-equity incentive compensation**, and **$124,188 in other compensation**; there was no separately reported discretionary cash bonus. [[2]] 

AMD set Su’s annualized base salary at **$1,323,000 effective December 27, 2025**, a **5.0%** increase from $1,260,000 a year earlier. [[1]] 

Her 2025 long-term equity grant had an intended target value of **$33.0 million**, comprising 151,283 target PRSUs and 102,516 options; its **$50.62 million** reported stock-plus-option value reflects ASC 718 grant-date accounting values in the summary compensation table. [[1, 3]] 

The $55.16 million reported compensation was **78% above FY2024’s $30.996 million**, and AMD states that approximately **96%** of its CEO’s target total direct compensation was variable or at risk. [[3, 1]]

**Bottom line:** Intel’s Gaudi program established a credible enterprise/OEM route to market, but its revenue ramp and cloud adoption materially underperformed Intel’s 2024 expectations; Intel has not publicly broken out an actual Gaudi revenue figure. [[1, 2]]

- **Revenue:** Intel targeted **$500 million of Gaudi revenue in 2024**, but CEO Pat Gelsinger said on the Q3 2024 earnings call that Intel would **not achieve that target**. [[1]]
- Intel’s public FY2024 disclosures list Gaudi processors among its hardware offerings but do not separately report Gaudi sales, so the defensible conclusion is **actual FY2024 revenue was below $500 million, not a precisely disclosed amount**. [[2, 1]]
- The weak ramp also had an accounting consequence: Intel’s FY2024 10-K discussion included **$922 million of Gaudi AI-accelerator inventory-related charges**, a significant sign that demand and inventory planning did not develop as anticipated. [[3]]

- **Why the ramp missed:** Management attributed the shortfall to slower-than-expected uptake amid the transition to Gaudi 3, while the commercial challenge was compounded by the need to sell a complete system/software experience rather than accelerator silicon alone. [[1, 4]]
- Intel’s FY2024 Q4 results also referred to inventory reserves related to Gaudi, consistent with the demand-conversion problem rather than a supply-constrained ramp. [[5]]

- **Initial adoption channel:** Intel made Gaudi 3 available to OEMs including **Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro** in Q2 2024, and announced customers/partners including IBM, NAVER, Bosch, Bharti Airtel, CtrlS, NielsenIQ, Roboflow and Seekr. [[6]]
- These announcements demonstrate ecosystem interest and qualification activity, but they should not be equated with high-volume deployments or meaningful reported revenue. [[6, 1]]

- **Most concrete commercial-adoption milestone:** In May 2025, IBM Cloud became the **first cloud service provider** to make Gaudi 3 available to customers, which Intel described as Gaudi 3’s **first major commercial deployment**. [[7]]
- Customers could access Gaudi 3 through IBM Cloud Virtual Servers on IBM VPC, with planned support for Red Hat OpenShift and IBM watsonx AI, improving the product’s enterprise-consumption model. [[7]]
- Intel also highlighted a Dell PowerEdge XE7740 configuration supporting up to eight double-wide accelerators, including Gaudi 3, and announced in May 2025 that Gaudi 3 was available in both PCIe and rack-scale systems. [[8] …[truncated]

[[4]] The disproportionate control reflects Mobileye’s dual-class structure: Class B shares carry **10 votes each**, versus one vote per Class A share. [[4]]

**Bottom line:** Mobileye is separately traded but not independently controlled: Intel retains decisive voting control, while Mobileye’s revenue base is predominantly tied to ADAS and autonomous-driving technology content supplied to automakers. [[1]] [[4]]

tool_arguments.query: Intel Gaudi AI accelerator revenue 2025

trajectory.content: Intel Gaudi AI accelerator revenue 2025

**Bottom line:** Intel’s Gaudi program established a credible enterprise/OEM route to market, but its revenue ramp and cloud adoption materially underperformed Intel’s 2024 expectations; Intel has not publicly broken out an actual Gaudi revenue figure. [[1, 2]]

- **Revenue:** Intel targeted **$500 million of Gaudi revenue in 2024**, but CEO Pat Gelsinger said on the Q3 2024 earnings call that Intel would **not achieve that target**. [[1]]
- Intel’s public FY2024 disclosures list Gaudi processors among its hardware offerings but do not separately report Gaudi sales, so the defensible conclusion is **actual FY2024 revenue was below $500 million, not a precisely disclosed amount**. [[2, 1]]
- The weak ramp also had an accounting consequence: Intel’s FY2024 10-K discussion included **$922 million of Gaudi AI-accelerator inventory-related charges**, a significant sign that demand and inventory planning did not develop as anticipated. [[3]]

- **Why the ramp missed:** Management attributed the shortfall to slower-than-expected uptake amid the transition to Gaudi 3, while the commercial challenge was compounded by the need to sell a complete system/software experience rather than accelerator silicon alone. [[1, 4]]
- Intel’s FY2024 Q4 results also referred to inventory reserves related to Gaudi, consistent with the demand-conversion problem rather than a supply-constrained ramp. [[5]]

- **Initial adoption channel:** Intel made Gaudi 3 available to OEMs including **Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro** in Q2 2024, and announced customers/partners including IBM, NAVER, Bosch, Bharti Airtel, CtrlS, NielsenIQ, Roboflow and Seekr. [[6]]
- These announcements demonstrate ecosystem interest and qualification activity, but they should not be equated with high-volume deployments or meaningful reported revenue. [[6, 1]]

- **Most concrete commercial-adoption milestone:** In May 2025, IBM Cloud became the **first cloud service provider** to make Gaudi 3 available to customers, which Intel described as Gaudi 3’s **first major commercial deployment**. [[7]]
- Customers could access Gaudi 3 through IBM Cloud Virtual Servers on IBM VPC, with planned support for Red Hat OpenShift and IBM watsonx AI, improving the product’s enterprise-consumption model. [[7]]
- Intel also highlighted a Dell PowerEdge XE7740 configuration supporting up to eight double-wide accelerators, including Gaudi 3, and announced in May 2025 that Gaudi 3 was available in both PCIe and rack-scale systems. [[8] …[truncated]

tool_arguments.query: Intel Gaudi AI accelerator revenue FY 2025 units shipped

trajectory.content: Intel Gaudi AI accelerator revenue FY 2025 units shipped

**Bottom line:** Intel’s Gaudi program established a credible enterprise/OEM route to market, but its revenue ramp and cloud adoption materially underperformed Intel’s 2024 expectations; Intel has not publicly broken out an actual Gaudi revenue figure. [[1, 2]]

- **Revenue:** Intel targeted **$500 million of Gaudi revenue in 2024**, but CEO Pat Gelsinger said on the Q3 2024 earnings call that Intel would **not achieve that target**. [[1]]
- Intel’s public FY2024 disclosures list Gaudi processors among its hardware offerings but do not separately report Gaudi sales, so the defensible conclusion is **actual FY2024 revenue was below $500 million, not a precisely disclosed amount**. [[2, 1]]
- The weak ramp also had an accounting consequence: Intel’s FY2024 10-K discussion included **$922 million of Gaudi AI-accelerator inventory-related charges**, a significant sign that demand and inventory planning did not develop as anticipated. [[3]]

- **Why the ramp missed:** Management attributed the shortfall to slower-than-expected uptake amid the transition to Gaudi 3, while the commercial challenge was compounded by the need to sell a complete system/software experience rather than accelerator silicon alone. [[1, 4]]
- Intel’s FY2024 Q4 results also referred to inventory reserves related to Gaudi, consistent with the demand-conversion problem rather than a supply-constrained ramp. [[5]]

- **Initial adoption channel:** Intel made Gaudi 3 available to OEMs including **Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro** in Q2 2024, and announced customers/partners including IBM, NAVER, Bosch, Bharti Airtel, CtrlS, NielsenIQ, Roboflow and Seekr. [[6]]
- These announcements demonstrate ecosystem interest and qualification activity, but they should not be equated with high-volume deployments or meaningful reported revenue. [[6, 1]]

- **Most concrete commercial-adoption milestone:** In May 2025, IBM Cloud became the **first cloud service provider** to make Gaudi 3 available to customers, which Intel described as Gaudi 3’s **first major commercial deployment**. [[7]]
- Customers could access Gaudi 3 through IBM Cloud Virtual Servers on IBM VPC, with planned support for Red Hat OpenShift and IBM watsonx AI, improving the product’s enterprise-consumption model. [[7]]
- Intel also highlighted a Dell PowerEdge XE7740 configuration supporting up to eight double-wide accelerators, including Gaudi 3, and announced in May 2025 that Gaudi 3 was available in both PCIe and rack-scale systems. [[8] …[truncated]

tool_arguments.query: Intel Gaudi AI accelerator revenue fiscal 2026

trajectory.content: Intel Gaudi AI accelerator revenue fiscal 2026

**Bottom line:** Intel’s Gaudi program established a credible enterprise/OEM route to market, but its revenue ramp and cloud adoption materially underperformed Intel’s 2024 expectations; Intel has not publicly broken out an actual Gaudi revenue figure. [[1, 2]]

- **Revenue:** Intel targeted **$500 million of Gaudi revenue in 2024**, but CEO Pat Gelsinger said on the Q3 2024 earnings call that Intel would **not achieve that target**. [[1]]
- Intel’s public FY2024 disclosures list Gaudi processors among its hardware offerings but do not separately report Gaudi sales, so the defensible conclusion is **actual FY2024 revenue was below $500 million, not a precisely disclosed amount**. [[2, 1]]
- The weak ramp also had an accounting consequence: Intel’s FY2024 10-K discussion included **$922 million of Gaudi AI-accelerator inventory-related charges**, a significant sign that demand and inventory planning did not develop as anticipated. [[3]]

- **Why the ramp missed:** Management attributed the shortfall to slower-than-expected uptake amid the transition to Gaudi 3, while the commercial challenge was compounded by the need to sell a complete system/software experience rather than accelerator silicon alone. [[1, 4]]
- Intel’s FY2024 Q4 results also referred to inventory reserves related to Gaudi, consistent with the demand-conversion problem rather than a supply-constrained ramp. [[5]]

- **Initial adoption channel:** Intel made Gaudi 3 available to OEMs including **Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro** in Q2 2024, and announced customers/partners including IBM, NAVER, Bosch, Bharti Airtel, CtrlS, NielsenIQ, Roboflow and Seekr. [[6]]
- These announcements demonstrate ecosystem interest and qualification activity, but they should not be equated with high-volume deployments or meaningful reported revenue. [[6, 1]]

- **Most concrete commercial-adoption milestone:** In May 2025, IBM Cloud became the **first cloud service provider** to make Gaudi 3 available to customers, which Intel described as Gaudi 3’s **first major commercial deployment**. [[7]]
- Customers could access Gaudi 3 through IBM Cloud Virtual Servers on IBM VPC, with planned support for Red Hat OpenShift and IBM watsonx AI, improving the product’s enterprise-consumption model. [[7]]
- Intel also highlighted a Dell PowerEdge XE7740 configuration supporting up to eight double-wide accelerators, including Gaudi 3, and announced in May 2025 that Gaudi 3 was available in both PCIe and rack-scale systems. [[8] …[truncated]

- **Broad-based AI-infrastructure buildout:** NVIDIA characterized demand as spanning hyperscalers, AI labs, AI-native companies, enterprises and sovereign customers, rather than depending on one customer group. [[2]]
- **Customer capex and cloud backlog:** NVIDIA cited cloud-industry backlog above **$2 trillion** and projected top-five-hyperscaler capex of nearly **$800 billion in 2026** and **$1.3 trillion in 2027**, supporting continued purchases of AI compute infrastructure. [[2]]

tool_arguments.query: Intel PC client segment revenue Q2 FY2026 Core Ultra laptops

trajectory.content: Intel PC client segment revenue Q2 FY2026 Core Ultra laptops

Intel does not separately disclose revenue from **Core Ultra laptops**; it reports the broader **Client Computing Group (CCG)** segment, which includes notebook, desktop and other client-platform revenue. [[1]] 

For FY2024, CCG generated **$30.3 billion** of revenue, up **4%** year over year; in Q4 2024, CCG revenue was **$8.0 billion**, down **9%** year over year. [[1]] 

The closest disclosed laptop-specific figure is CCG **notebook revenue**: **$4.888 billion in Q3 2024**, versus $4.503 billion in Q3 2023. [[2]] 

Core Ultra is a processor product family rather than a reported revenue segment: Intel said more than **5 million AI PCs** had shipped since the December 2023 Core Ultra launch as of Q1 2024, but that shipment statistic is not equivalent to Core Ultra laptop revenue. [[3]] 

For context, CCG revenue was **$32.2 billion in FY2025**, down 3% from the prior year, including **$8.2 billion in Q4 2025**, down 7% year over year. [[4]]

For FY2024, CCG generated **$30.3 billion** of revenue, up **4%** year over year; in Q4 2024, CCG revenue was **$8.0 billion**, down **9%** year over year. [[1]] 

The closest disclosed laptop-specific figure is CCG **notebook revenue**: **$4.888 billion in Q3 2024**, versus $4.503 billion in Q3 2023. [[2]] 

Core Ultra is a processor product family rather than a reported revenue segment: Intel said more than **5 million AI PCs** had shipped since the December 2023 Core Ultra launch as of Q1 2024, but that shipment statistic is not equivalent to Core Ultra laptop revenue. [[3]] 

For context, CCG revenue was **$32.2 billion in FY2025**, down 3% from the prior year, including **$8.2 billion in Q4 2025**, down 7% year over year. [[4]]

## GeForce vs. Radeon: gaming benchmark comparison

The short version: **Radeon is generally stronger for native-rasterized gaming value, while GeForce is generally stronger for ray tracing**, with NVIDIA also offering the more mature DLSS/frame-generation ecosystem. [[1]] 

The benchmark figures below are Tom’s Hardware multi-game averages at **native resolution, Ultra settings, with no DLSS, FSR, XeSS, or frame generation enabled**, so they isolate underlying GPU performance rather than upscaler quality. [[1]]

| Performance tier | Native 1440p Ultra raster average | Ray-traced 1440p Ultra average | Practical comparison |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Flagship | RTX 5090: 167.3 fps; RTX 4090: 143.4 fps; RTX 5080: 128.3 fps; RX 7900 XTX: 122.3 fps | RTX 5090: 100.8 fps; RTX 4090: 87.7 fps; RTX 5080: 74.0 fps; RX 7900 XTX: 50.5 fps | NVIDIA’s top cards lead decisively once heavy ray tracing is enabled, while the 7900 XTX remains competitive in conventional raster games. [[1]] [[2]]|
| Upper-midrange | RTX 5070 Ti: 116.8 fps; RX 9070 XT: 116.5 fps; RX 9070: 104.0 fps; RTX 5070: 96.4 fps | RTX 5070 Ti: 66.2 fps; RX 9070 XT: 55.5 fps; RTX 5070: 51.5 fps; RX 9070: 47.6 fps | The RX 9070 XT essentially matches the RTX 5070 Ti in native 1440p rasterization despite its lower $599 MSRP, but the GeForce card leads in ray tracing. [[1]] [[2]]|
| Mainstream | RX 9060 XT and RTX 5060 compete closely at 1080p performance per dollar | NVIDIA retains an architectural advantage in ray-traced workloads, though the exact gap depends substantially on the game and settings. [[1]]|

### What the benchmarks imply

- **For 1080p or 1440p gaming without ray tracing:** Radeon is usually the more compelling value choice, particularly the RX 9070 at 1440p; Tom’s Hardware identifies it as the current 1440p raster-value leader, ahead of the RX 9070 GRE and RTX 5070. [[1]]

- **For ray tracing:** choose GeForce where prices are comparable, especially in the higher tiers; at 1440p RT Ultra, the RTX 5070 Ti averages 66.2 fps versus 55.5 fps for the RX 9070 XT, and the RTX 5080 averages 74.0 fps versus 50.5 fps for the RX 7900 XTX. [[2]]

- **For a roughly $550–$600 1440p build:** the RX 9070 XT is the raster-first choice at $599 MSRP and 116.5 fps at 1440p Ultra, while the RTX 5070 costs $549 MSRP, averages 96.4 fps in rasterization, and is modestly ahead in 1440p ray tracing at 51.5 fps versus 47.6 fps for the RX 9070. [[1]] [[2]]

trajectory.content: NVIDIA Q2 FY2027 gross profit and revenue breakdown by segment

**NVIDIA Data Center revenue was $89.0 billion in Q2 FY2027** (quarter ended July 26, 2026), increasing **18% sequentially** and **117% year over year**; it represented about **92.5%** of total company revenue of $96.2 billion. [[1]]

**Primary growth drivers**

- **Blackwell Ultra infrastructure ramp:** NVIDIA’s 10-Q identifies the ramp of Blackwell Ultra as the direct driver of Data Center growth, while Blackwell accounted for the majority of system shipments. [[2]]
- **Broad hyperscaler demand:** Hyperscale Data Center revenue reached **$48.7 billion**, up **13% QoQ** and **102% YoY**, driven by sustained strength in Blackwell/Blackwell Ultra deployments. [[2]]
- **Faster growth outside traditional hyperscalers:** AI Clouds, Industrial & Enterprise (“ACIE”) revenue rose to **$40.3 billion**, up **25% QoQ** and **138% YoY**, pointing to incremental demand from neoclouds, AI-model makers, industrial customers, and enterprises. [[2, 3]]
- **AI-infrastructure buildout widened across customer types:** NVIDIA characterized demand as extending across hyperscalers, AI labs, AI-native firms, enterprises, and sovereign customers, supported by an expanding global AI-infrastructure buildout. [[3]]
- **More valuable full-system content per gigawatt:** NVIDIA’s platform extends beyond GPUs to CPUs, NVLink, and InfiniBand/Ethernet networking; management said the revenue opportunity increased from roughly **$18 billion/GW for Hopper** to **$25 billion/GW for Grace Blackwell**, increasing revenue content as customers deploy AI factories. [[3]]
- **China was not material to the result:** Hopper Data Center sales to China were less than **1% of Data Center revenue** in the quarter, so the growth was principally generated elsewhere. [[2]]

**Bottom line:** Q2 FY2027 growth was not solely a unit-volume rebound—it reflected the Blackwell Ultra product-cycle ramp, accelerating purchases by hyperscalers, outsized expansion in neocloud/enterprise/industrial demand, and higher platform content per AI data-center deployment. [[2, 3]]

trajectory.content: Intel Gaudi AI accelerator revenue fiscal 2026

**Bottom line:** Intel’s Gaudi program established a credible enterprise/OEM route to market, but its revenue ramp and cloud adoption materially underperformed Intel’s 2024 expectations; Intel has not publicly broken out an actual Gaudi revenue figure. [[1, 2]]

- **Revenue:** Intel targeted **$500 million of Gaudi revenue in 2024**, but CEO Pat Gelsinger said on the Q3 2024 earnings call that Intel would **not achieve that target**. [[1]]
- Intel’s public FY2024 disclosures list Gaudi processors among its hardware offerings but do not separately report Gaudi sales, so the defensible conclusion is **actual FY2024 revenue was below $500 million, not a precisely disclosed amount**. [[2, 1]]
- The weak ramp also had an accounting consequence: Intel’s FY2024 10-K discussion included **$922 million of Gaudi AI-accelerator inventory-related charges**, a significant sign that demand and inventory planning did not develop as anticipated. [[3]]

- **Why the ramp missed:** Management attributed the shortfall to slower-than-expected uptake amid the transition to Gaudi 3, while the commercial challenge was compounded by the need to sell a complete system/software experience rather than accelerator silicon alone. [[1, 4]]
- Intel’s FY2024 Q4 results also referred to inventory reserves related to Gaudi, consistent with the demand-conversion problem rather than a supply-constrained ramp. [[5]]

- **Initial adoption channel:** Intel made Gaudi 3 available to OEMs including **Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro** in Q2 2024, and announced customers/partners including IBM, NAVER, Bosch, Bharti Airtel, CtrlS, NielsenIQ, Roboflow and Seekr. [[6]]
- These announcements demonstrate ecosystem interest and qualification activity, but they should not be equated with high-volume deployments or meaningful reported revenue. [[6, 1]]

- **Revenue:** Intel targeted **$500 million of Gaudi revenue in 2024**, but CEO Pat Gelsinger said on the Q3 2024 earnings call that Intel would **not achieve that target**. [[1]]
- Intel’s public FY2024 disclosures list Gaudi processors among its hardware offerings but do not separately report Gaudi sales, so the defensible conclusion is **actual FY2024 revenue was below $500 million, not a precisely disclosed amount**. [[2, 1]]
- The weak ramp also had an accounting consequence: Intel’s FY2024 10-K discussion included **$922 million of Gaudi AI-accelerator inventory-related charges**, a significant sign that demand and inventory planning did not develop as anticipated. [[3]]

- **Why the ramp missed:** Management attributed the shortfall to slower-than-expected uptake amid the transition to Gaudi 3, while the commercial challenge was compounded by the need to sell a complete system/software experience rather than accelerator silicon alone. [[1, 4]]
- Intel’s FY2024 Q4 results also referred to inventory reserves related to Gaudi, consistent with the demand-conversion problem rather than a supply-constrained ramp. [[5]]
